subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: “Sit, child, sit. When my father died I was twenty-six, and the three of us grieved so differently that we nearly broke as a family. My brother Parveen took charge of every form, every phone call and every chair for the guests. My sister Tashi talked about our father all night, telling the same stories again and again. I said almost nothing and sat by the window. Tashi said, ‘Dolma doesn't even miss him.’ Parveen said, ‘Tashi is only making noise.’ Each thought the others were doing it wrong. On the eleventh night Parveen stopped in the doorway with a file in his hand and said, ‘I don't know how to sit.’ We all laughed and cried at once. That night we finally sat together.”

qa.q: How old was Dolma when the father died?
qa.a: Dolma was twenty-six when the father died.

qa.q: What might Parveen have meant when Parveen said, “I don't know how to sit”?
qa.a: Parveen probably felt that tasks were the only way to cope with the loss, and being still was frightening, so he admitted it finally.

qa.q: What could the three have done sooner to lessen the hurt?
qa.a: They could have asked each other how each was coping, and understood that quiet, talking and busy work were all ways of grieving.

qa.q: How might Tashi have felt when Tashi said, “Dolma doesn't even miss him”?
qa.a: Tashi may have felt lonely in the storytelling and frustrated that others were not joining in, and so read Dolma's silence as not caring.

grounding: An elder recalls a family whose members grieved quietly, by talking and by staying busy, each thinking the others were doing it wrong, until they understood.

subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: The storm cut the power the night after their mother's funeral, and the three grown-up children were stuck in the old house with no phone signal. Aparna sat by the window with a candle, silent. Chinmay hunted through drawers for the property papers and bank documents. “We have to do this while everyone's here,” he said. Their younger sister Riya talked and talked, going through old photographs. “You're not even sad, Aparna,” Riya said. “And you're not doing anything useful,” said Chinmay. Aparna looked at them both. “I am sad. I don't know how to say it in your way.” Chinmay put down the files. Riya went quiet. Chinmay held the candle while Aparna lifted the photo album.

qa.q: What did Chinmay search for in the drawers?
qa.a: Chinmay hunted through drawers for the property papers and bank documents.

qa.q: Why did Aparna say, “I am sad. I don't know how to say it in your way”?
qa.a: Aparna felt misjudged, since silence looked like not grieving to the other two, and wanted them to understand that the sadness was real.

qa.q: What might the three do next to grieve better together?
qa.a: They could take turns, with a little time for papers and a little for the photographs and silence, so each style of grieving has room.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Chinmay put down the files?
qa.a: Chinmay may have felt a mixture of shame and relief at seeing Aparna's grief, and realised the papers could wait a little.

grounding: A family member grieves quietly while another talks and another keeps busy with tasks, each thinking the others are not grieving properly.
